summary: Describes the RObust Header Compression framework, an efficient and flexible way of shrinking packet headers over many link types. It separates the framework and the profile for uncompressed from RFC 3095. It was replaced by RFC 5795.

questions: how does rohc detect context damage
how does rohc handle packet loss
subtitle: Efficient and robust header compression for wireless and lossy links.

tldr.problem: Packet headers are large (40-60 bytes for TCP/IP/RTP), and on wireless links with high loss and long round-trip times, legacy compression schemes like CRTP fail because lost packets cause context damage and subsequent decompression failures.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC (RObust Header Compression) separates the framework from profiles, uses CICs (context identifiers) to track flows, detects and repairs context damage with CRCs and feedback, and handles reordering and residual errors robustly.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 5795, which refined the specification.

today: RFC 4995 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 5795, which refined the ROHC framework specification.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Internet packets carry multiple headers—IP, TCP or UDP, and often RTP for audio/video. For IPv4, this totals 40 bytes; IPv6 adds another 20. On wireless links and IP tunnels where bandwidth is precious and packet loss common, this header overhead is significant, especially for small payloads like 20-byte voice packets. Header compression reduces this overhead by using the redundancy between consecutive packets.

Earlier schemes like CTCP, IPHC, and CRTP work well on reliable links but fail on lossy links because lost packets corrupt the compression context (the state both sides use to compress/decompress). Robust Header Compression (ROHC) solves this by explicitly handling context damage with error detection and repair mechanisms like CRCs and feedback, designed from the start for wireless networks.
sections.eli5: Old compression breaks when packets get lost on wireless. ROHC is designed to notice when something breaks and fix itself instead of giving up.

sections.title: How Header Compression Works
sections.content:
Header compression exploits the fact that header field values repeat across packets in the same flow. Some fields stay the same throughout a flow (static), some change predictably (like a sequence number incrementing by one each time), and some are inferred from context or layer information.

The compressor learns the change pattern of each field and sends full values initially, then only the changes. The decompressor maintains the same context (state) and reconstructs headers from compressed representations. When the compressor and decompressor contexts become inconsistent due to lost packets, decompression fails. ROHC prevents and repairs this through periodic context refreshes, error-detection codes, and feedback from the decompressor about what it successfully received.
sections.eli5: If an address never changes, you only say it once. If it increases by one each time, you only send the increase. The trick is keeping both sides in sync when signals drop.

sections.title: The ROHC Channel, Contexts, and Flows
sections.content:
A ROHC channel is a logical unidirectional path carrying compressed packets and optionally feedback in the opposite direction. A packet flow is a sequence of packets (identified by addresses, ports, and protocol) that can share a compression context. Each flow is assigned a Context Identifier (CID), a short label sent with compressed headers so the decompressor knows which context to use.

The CID space is negotiated at channel setup: small (0-15, requiring no overhead for CID 0) or large (0-16383). A channel also defines the set of compression profiles both sides support—profiles define how to compress specific protocol combinations like UDP/RTP. Contexts can be static (fields that never change) or dynamic (fields that change), organized separately in the decompressor's memory for efficiency.
sections.eli5: The channel is the pipe. Flows are the different conversations in the pipe. Each one gets a number tag (CID) so the other side knows what context to use. Both sides agree which compression tricks to use before sending anything.

sections.title: Packet Types and Error Detection
sections.content:
ROHC defines packet types for different situations. IR (Initialization and Refresh) packets send full uncompressed header information to establish or refresh context. IR-DYN packets refresh only the dynamic part of the context. CO (Compressed) packets send only the changes, identified by profile-specific type codes. Feedback packets carry ACKs or NACKs from decompressor to compressor.

All compressed packets include error-detection codes: an 8-bit CRC in IR headers validates the entire context, and 3-bit or 7-bit CRCs in compressed headers verify decompression. If verification fails, the decompressor sends negative feedback (NACK) requesting refresh. Segmentation handles compressed headers larger than the link MTU by splitting them across multiple frames with a reassembly mechanism.
sections.eli5: Full header packets (IR) let you set up or fix the context. Compressed packets (CO) are tiny. If the tiny one looks broken, you ask for a full one. The decompressor checks each packet's math to spot corruption.

sections.title: Robustness and Operational Characteristics
sections.content:
ROHC profiles achieve robustness through several mechanisms. Master Sequence Numbers (MSN) tied to one of the protocol fields (like RTP sequence number) let the decompressor detect out-of-order delivery. CRC validation detects bit errors introduced during transmission. Feedback allows decompressor-initiated repair: upon detecting context damage, the decompressor sends NACK feedback to trigger an IR refresh.

The RFC defines three key robustness levels for different link characteristics. Legacy ROHC profiles (from RFC 3095) assume in-order delivery between compressor and decompressor. ROHCv2 profiles (newer) handle out-of-order delivery. All assume the link provides framing, no packet duplication, and error detection at lower layers. Compression efficiency is traded against robustness and transparency—extra CRC overhead and refresh frequency impact compression ratio but improve reliability.
sections.eli5: The compressor adds math checks to packets so the decompressor spots corruption. If something looks wrong, the decompressor says so, and the compressor sends a full header. The fancy versions can handle packets arriving out of order.

sections.title: Profiles and Extensibility
sections.content:
A ROHC profile is a compression protocol for specific header combinations. The framework defines a null Uncompressed profile (ID 0x0000) that passes headers uncompressed but still uses the channel mechanisms for flow multiplexing and feedback. Actual compression profiles (defined in companion documents) build on the framework by specifying encoding methods for the protocol headers they target, such as RTP/UDP/IP or TCP/IP.

The framework explicitly separates the framework specification from profile specifications, clarifying which rules apply to all profiles versus profile-specific rules. This makes the specification less complex and makes it easier to add new profiles in the future. The framework reserves certain packet type identifiers for common purposes and leaves others available for profiles to define their own types.
sections.eli5: The framework is the basic rules: how to set up, how to detect errors, how to ask for help. Profiles add the specifics of what to compress for each protocol. You can write new profiles without changing the framework.
